text: Ephraim has surrounded me with lies, the house of Israel with deceit; but Judah still walks with God and is faithful to the Holy One.[fn] \n[fn] The Hebrew of this line is uncertain; it may also be read, "Judah is still unruly toward God, toward the Holy One who is faithful."

versions.text: Ephraim has surrounded me with lies, the house of Israel with deceit; but Judah still walks with God and is faithful to the Holy One.
versions.explanation: The verb רָד is textually and lexically ambiguous, and the verse is read by some as praise of Judah and by others as an indictment. Since the choice affects the theology of the passage, a brief footnote noting the alternative reading would serve the reader without changing the main text.

text: Ephraim herds the wind and chases the east wind all day long; he piles up lies and violence. They make a treaty with Assyria, and oil is carried down to Egypt.
The LORD has a case against Judah; he will call Jacob to account for his ways and repay him for what he has done.
In the womb he grasped his brother's heel, and in his strength he wrestled with God.
He struggled with the angel and prevailed; he wept and pleaded for his favor. At Bethel he found him, and there he spoke with us—
the LORD, the God of hosts; the LORD is his name.
So you must return to your God. Hold fast to mercy and justice, and wait for your God without ceasing.
A merchant with false scales in his hand—he loves to defraud.[fn] \n[fn] Hebrew: "Canaan," a name used for traders and merchants.

versions.text: A merchant with false scales in his hand—he loves to defraud.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew word here is literally "Canaan," used as a byword for traders; a short footnote preserves the wordplay and the allusion to Israel behaving like the Canaanites, which is otherwise invisible in the English.

text: Ephraim says, "How rich I have become! I have gained wealth for myself. In all my toil no one can find any guilt in me, any sin."

versions.text: Ephraim says, "How rich I have become! I have made a fortune for myself. In all my gain no one can find in me guilt that is sin."
versions.explanation: "Guilt that is sin" is a stiff calque that reads awkwardly aloud; the Hebrew doubles the terms for emphasis, which is better rendered as two parallel phrases. יְגִיעַי refers to Ephraim's labor/toil rather than to his "gain," which duplicates the preceding line.

text: But I am the LORD your God from the land of Egypt; I will make you live in tents again, as in the days of the appointed feast.
I spoke to the prophets; I multiplied visions, and through the prophets I gave parables.
If Gilead is full of iniquity, they are nothing but falsehood. In Gilgal they sacrifice bulls; their altars, too, are like heaps of stones on the furrows of a field.

versions.text: If Gilead is worthless, they have come to nothing at all. In Gilgal they sacrifice bulls; their altars, too, are like heaps of stones on the furrows of a field.
versions.explanation: אָוֶן means "iniquity/wickedness," not "worthless," and the parallel שָׁוְא ("falsehood, emptiness") is what carries the sense of nothingness. As it stands, the two halves of the line say nearly the same thing and the moral indictment of Gilead is lost.

text: Jacob fled to the land of Aram; Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he tended sheep.
By a prophet the LORD brought Israel up from Egypt, and by a prophet Israel was kept.
Ephraim has provoked him bitterly; so his blood will remain upon him, and his Lord will bring his own disgrace back upon him.

versions.text: Ephraim has given bitter provocation; so his Lord will leave his bloodguilt upon him and repay him for his contempt.
versions.explanation: חֶרְפָּתוֹ means "his reproach/disgrace" — the shame Ephraim has earned is turned back on him — rather than "his contempt," which shifts the noun's meaning to Ephraim's attitude. "Bloodguilt" is an interpretive expansion of דָּמָיו; "his blood" with "remain upon him" conveys the idiom more directly.
